content.title: About
content.content: Ketchup is a thick sauce made from tomato puree, vinegar, sugar, and spices. It has a sweet‑sour flavor and is used as a condiment for a wide range of dishes, from fries to burgers.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first commercial ketchup was created in the United States in 1876 by the Heinz company.
The classic recipe includes tomatoes, vinegar, sugar, salt, and spices such as cloves, cinnamon, and allspice.
Different countries have their own variations: Japan adds soy sauce, India adds curry spices.
Ketchup is often used in culinary experiments, for example in marinades or barbecue sauces.
There are gluten‑free and sugar‑free versions for diet‑restricted consumers.

items.title: Source of lycopene
items.content: Tomatoes used to make ketchup are rich in lycopene, an antioxidant that supports heart health.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals
items.content: Ketchup provides small amounts of vitamin C, vitamin A, and potassium.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Unlike many sauces, ketchup contains virtually no fat.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Traditional ketchup often contains a lot of sugar, which can contribute to weight gain and raise blood glucose levels.

items.title: Sodium level
items.content: A high amount of salt may be problematic for people with hypertension.

items.title: Allergens
items.content: Some recipes include spices that can trigger allergic reactions.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve ketchup with fried, baked, or boiled dishes, use it as a base for sauces, marinades, and salad dressings. It can be added to burgers, hot dogs, sandwiches, or used in culinary experiments.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store ketchup in the refrigerator after opening, in a tightly sealed container. At room temperature it can last several weeks, but flavor and quality are best preserved when kept cold.
